title: 5 Things I Wish I Knew When I Started Project Management
author: The Effective Project Manager
summary: An engineer who drifted into project management reflects on five things he wishes he had known at the start. His central claim is that the job is far more about people than technique: he rarely looks at KPIs but spends every day communicating with upset, confused or disappointed people and trying to win them over. He adds that structured professional development is almost nonexistent once you are working, so a manager has to own his own growth. The piece then turns to the inner side of managing, arguing that stress comes from uncertainty, that delays should be planned for and disclosed to stakeholders rather than denied, and that satisfaction from a finished project is fleeting so you must manufacture your own along the way. It is a short, candid practitioner's list, but it hangs together as a view of what managing a team and its stakeholders actually demands.
points: Managing is mostly a people job: daily communication with upset or confused stakeholders outweighs KPI tracking, and the author wishes he had been trained for it.
Professional development is not supplied by employers, so a manager must deliberately choose mentors, sites and courses to keep growing.
Stress is traced to uncertainty, and the remedy offered is to cling to controllable certainties such as process, routine and predictable behaviour.
Delay is treated as a certainty on any complex project, so leaders should plan to absorb it and tell stakeholders that slippage happens.
Because success moments are rare and brief, leaders should build their own job satisfaction through celebrating team wins and journaling what they are proud of.
quotes: The first thing to know is that it’s much less about technical skills and much more about people skills. Think it’s all about KPI’s? I hardly look at them.
In essence, I spend time trying to get people on my side. That is the biggest part of the job. I wish I’d known that going in, and I really wish I’d been trained in it.

Once you’re in a career, with the exception of a very few small companies, almost no structured, formal professional development happens. You do your work. You are expected to do your work and to just keep doing your work.
The third thing I learned quickly is that stress comes from uncertainty. There’s so much that we know about projects, but there’s so much that we don’t.
To keep myself sane, I need to cling to whatever certainties I can find. In processes. In routine. In trying to be predictable in my actions.
Delays are inevitable and I am yet to meet a project that hasn’t been delayed. If the project has even more than just a wee tiny bit of complexity, delay is guaranteed.
Perhaps the biggest thing I learned is that you need to make your own job satisfaction. Project successful happens seldom, and the satisfaction that you get from it is very fleeting.
